title: Forecasting: start with the calendar
subtitle: What does a forecast have to know to beat 'same as last week'?
goal: After this lesson you can direct a forecast in the right order: naive baselines first, then a model that names the trend, the weekly and yearly rhythm and the known event dates, and you can check what it found against what you already know.

predict.q: Copying the same weekday from last week forward misses daily platform spend by about 6 percent on this series. A model that is told the trend, the weekday, the time of year and the holiday dates removes how much of that error?
options: Almost none: the rest is noise
About a fifth of it
More than half of it
Nearly all of it
predict.reveal: More than half: about 6 percent falls to under 3. The lesson shows which ingredient buys what, and why this is a best case.

segments.narration: It is the last week of the month and finance wants a number: platform spend, day by day, for the next four weeks. The quickest answer in the building is, same as last week. That is not a silly answer. It is a baseline, the forecasting cousin of predicting that everyone stays. So what does a forecast have to know to beat it, and by how much? Our series is simulated daily spend for a whole platform, 851 days of it, so we know exactly what went into it.

visual.title: Forecasting: start with the calendar
visual.sub: Trend, rhythm and the dates you already know

segments.narration: Pull the series apart and you find four ingredients and a leftover. [[1]] A trend: growth of about 15 percent a year. [[2]] A weekly rhythm: weekends run roughly 20 percent below weekdays. [[3]] A yearly rhythm: spend sags through spring and summer, then climbs to a peak in late November. [[4]] Known events: Black Friday week, Christmas, New Year's Day. [[5]] The leftover is noise, the wobble no method can forecast. None of this is machine learning yet. It is the calendar, and you could find most of it with a GROUP BY on weekday, month and year. The idea is general: any daily count, say next month's support tickets for staffing, is forecast from its trend, its rhythm and its known dates.

visual.title: What is in 851 days of platform spend
items: Year: low in March, peak in late November
Known events: Black Friday week, Christmas, New Year's Day

segments.narration: Start with three naive forecasts. Each predicts the next 28 days from the first of a month, twelve months running. The score is the average daily miss, as a percentage of that day's actual spend. [[1]] Carry the last day's value forward and you are off by about 14 percent a day: the last day you saw may be a Friday, and tomorrow is a Saturday. [[2]] Use the same weekday from last week instead, and the miss falls to about 6 percent. More than half the error was the weekly rhythm. [[3]] Average the last four of each weekday and it improves a little more. Its worst month is far milder too: one unusual week is no longer copied forward alone.

visual.title: Naive forecasts: average daily error (MAPE), 28 days ahead
visual.note: Worst of the twelve months: 27.3%, 23.6% and 9.8%.

segments.narration: Now give a model those ingredients by name. [[1]] It is the weighted sum from module three, fitted on the log of spend: a trend, an effect for each weekday, a smooth curve for the time of year, and a flag for each known event. [[2]] It trains only on days before the forecast date, then predicts the next 28. [[3]] Its average daily miss is under 3 percent, about half that of the best naive method, and its worst month is barely worse than its average. A boosted tree model given the same calendar columns manages about 5 percent, level with the four week average.

visual.title: A model that names the calendar
lines: log(spend) = trend + weekday + time of year + event dates
trained only on days before the forecast date
average daily error 2.8%  ·  best naive method 5.7%
visual.note: Worst month 3.5%. Boosted trees on the same calendar columns: 5.4%.

segments.narration: The model is readable, which a copied week is not. [[1]] It found growth of about 15 percent a year, the rate that was built into the series. [[3]] Saturdays and Sundays around a fifth below Mondays. [[4]] Black Friday week about 22 percent up. [[6]] Christmas and New Year's Day down by a fifth to a quarter. Because it works on the log scale, these effects multiply, as they did in the spend model from module three. Each of those is something you can check against a dashboard you already own, and argue about with finance.

visual.title: What the model found
visual.note: Fitted on log spend, so the effects multiply.

segments.narration: Now take one ingredient away: fit the same model without the event dates. [[1]] With them, the average miss was 2.8 percent and the worst month 3.5. [[2]] Without them the average barely moves, to 3.3 percent. But the worst month climbs to 6.3, close to double. An average can hide a holiday; the worst month cannot. Nothing in the rhythm of the data tells a model that one particular week in late November is special. Somebody has to say so. The calendar is where your domain knowledge goes in, the way features were in module four.

visual.title: Same model, with and without the event dates

segments.narration: Before you quote 2.8 percent, look at where it came from. This series has a version with seven planted incidents, kept for a later lesson. These scores use the version without them, so forecast error is not mixed up with outage days. And this world is stable by construction, with a model of the same form as the equation that generated it. It was even handed the holiday dates. That is a best case, and a real series, with breaks nobody planned, will score worse. What carries over is the order of work, not the number. Now try it: one forecast, made on the first of March. Switch between the methods and see where each parts from what happened.

segments.narration: The brief. Ask the assistant to work in this order, and make the output prove each step. [[1]] Baselines first: same weekday last week, and the average of the last four. [[2]] Then the model, with event dates that you supply and it lists back. [[3]] Every method scored on the same forecast dates, each trained only on earlier days. [[4]] The worst month beside the average. [[5]] And the fitted effects in percent: growth per year, the weekend dip, each event. If the weekend dip it reports is not the one on your dashboard, stop there. And for a small decision a few weeks out, a four week average in a spreadsheet, adjusted by hand for known events, will do.

segments.narration: Next time finance asks for a number, you know the order of work, and most of the ingredients are already on your dashboards and calendar. Next lesson: testing a forecast from a past date forward, and giving a range, not one number.

visual.text: Most of a forecast is calendar: trend, rhythm and the dates you already know.
visual.sub: Baselines first. Then name the ingredients.

takeaways: Ask for naive baselines first: the same weekday last week, and the average of the last four.
Most of a forecast is trend, weekly and yearly rhythm, and known event dates; a model that names them can be read and checked.
Event dates are knowledge only you can supply, and a score from a stable simulated series is a best case.

quiz.q: An analyst forecasts the next four weeks of platform spend by carrying the last day's value forward, and reports an average daily miss of 14 percent. A colleague concludes that the series is simply too noisy to forecast. What is the better read?
options: The colleague is right: a miss of 14 percent is noise, and no method can remove noise from a series
Most of that miss is the weekly rhythm: score 'same weekday last week' before blaming noise
The series needs a more flexible model with many more columns before the noise can be cut through
A longer average is the fix: forecast each day as the mean of the last 30 days
quiz.why: One day's value says nothing about which weekday is being forecast: on this series, copying the same weekday from last week cut the miss from about 14 to about 6 percent with no model at all. A 30-day mean still predicts the same value for a Saturday as for a Wednesday, so the rhythm that caused the miss is still unaccounted for.

quiz.concept: known events and the worst month
quiz.q: The assistant's report says: 'Calendar model: average daily error 3.3 percent over twelve monthly forecasts, against 6.4 percent for the baseline.' The features listed are trend, weekday and time of year. What do you ask for before this goes to finance?
options: The worst month, and a rerun with the known event dates added: an average can hide a holiday
The same average over twenty-four monthly forecasts instead of twelve, to make 3.3 percent steadier
The same test with a more complex model, to see whether the error can be pushed lower still
The error restated in dollars, because finance cannot act on a percentage
quiz.why: The feature list has no event dates, and that gap does not show in an average: on this series leaving them out moved the average only from 2.8 to 3.3 percent but nearly doubled the worst month. A more complex model, or a steadier average, chases the same number while the hole in the feature list stays open.

quiz.q: The support lead needs daily ticket volumes for next month's staffing. In the history, Mondays run far above Fridays, volume drifts up month after month, and it jumps whenever a product release ships. The assistant proposes forecasting every day as the average of the last 30 days. What is missing?
options: A longer window: a 90-day average would smooth out the release jumps and give staffing a steadier level
History: several more years of data are needed before any of these patterns can be trusted
The three things already known to be in the series: the weekday pattern, the drift, the releases
Power: a pattern this complex needs a neural network, not an average
quiz.why: The weekday pattern, the drift and the release calendar are the ingredients a forecast should name; a flat average predicts the same volume for a Monday as for a Friday and knows nothing about the next release. More history, a longer average or a bigger model does not help while those ingredients are still left out.

quiz.q: On the simulated series the regression missed by under 3 percent a day. A stakeholder asks what accuracy to expect from the same approach on the real platform next quarter. What is the honest answer?
options: About the same, under 3 percent: the method is identical, so its accuracy carries over
Better than 3 percent, provided the real model is given more columns than the simulated one had
Better than 3 percent, because the real platform has many more years of history to learn from
Worse, by an amount nobody knows yet: rehearse on your own history and quote that number
quiz.why: The simulated series never changes its behaviour and the model has the same form as the equation behind it, so under 3 percent is a best case, not a prediction of your accuracy. The method carries over; the number has to be measured on your own data.

variants.q: A new model for daily platform spend reports an average miss of 5.5 percent on its test forecasts. What do you need to see before deciding whether that is good?
options: Whether 5.5 percent is under the 10 percent that is generally taken to mean a good forecast
What 'same weekday last week' and a four-week weekday average score on the same dates
How many columns the model was given, since more columns mean a better forecast
Whether the model is a regression or is built from trees
variants.why: A forecast error means nothing without the cheap alternatives beside it: on the course series a four-week weekday average already scores 5.7 percent, so 5.5 would be almost no gain. There is no universal percentage that makes a forecast good.

variants.q: A client's e-commerce team forecasts daily orders with a model that misses by 9 percent on average. Orders run much higher at weekends. Which comparison tells you whether the model earns its keep?
options: Its error on the period it was trained on, where the model has the most data to work with
Last year's total orders divided by 365, used as the forecast for every day
A second, more complex model's error on the same days, to see which one wins
The same weekday last week, scored on the same days as the model
variants.why: With a strong weekly rhythm the fair bar is a baseline that already knows the weekday; if copying last week scores 9 percent too, the model adds nothing. Error on the training period flatters any model and is not a comparison at all.

variants.q: A team shows a forecast of weekly new-advertiser sign-ups and says its error is 12 percent. Sign-ups have grown steadily all year. What is the natural naive forecast to demand beside it?
options: Last week's figure carried forward, perhaps with the recent weekly growth added
The average of every week since the platform launched, which uses the most data
A random draw from the range the series has covered in the past
The team's own target for weekly sign-ups, since that is what the forecast serves
variants.why: For a weekly series the cheap forecast is 'same as last week', possibly nudged by recent growth; a model has to beat that to be worth running. An all-time average ignores the growth, lands far too low, and would make almost any model look brilliant.

review.concept: known event dates are domain knowledge

variants.q: A spend forecast is accurate most of the year, yet every year it misses badly in the week of a large shopping event. The model has a trend, weekday effects and smooth yearly terms. What is the best fix?
options: Add a flag for the event's dates, taken from the business calendar
Add several more years of history and let the model discover the event by itself
Switch to a more flexible algorithm that can bend around the event
Drop that week from the evaluation as an outlier
variants.why: Smooth yearly terms cannot single out one particular week, so the model has to be told the dates; then it can learn the size of the effect. Dropping the week from the evaluation hides the miss in exactly the week the business cares about most.

variants.q: A sports advertiser's daily spend surges on days with a big televised match. Match days are announced weeks ahead but fall on no fixed weekday. Your forecast of that account's spend misses every one of them. What should you ask the assistant to do?
options: Smooth the history so that the match-day surges no longer distort the average
Add the match dates, past and announced, as an input to the forecast
Train only on weeks that had no match, to keep the pattern clean
Strengthen the weekly rhythm terms until they absorb the surges
variants.why: Match dates are known in advance to anyone who looks, but they are invisible in the weekday and the month: given as an input, past matches teach the size of the surge and announced ones place it. Smoothing or excluding those days teaches the model that match days do not exist.

variants.q: An education client's lead volume drops sharply during school holidays, whose dates shift each year and differ by region. A forecast built on weekday and month of year keeps missing them. Why, and what fixes it?
options: The model is memorising; remove the month term and the problem goes away
Lead volume is simply too noisy to forecast during school holidays
Month of year cannot follow dates that move; supply the holiday calendar for each region
Daily data is the problem; forecast yearly totals, which do not depend on holiday timing
variants.why: A month term assumes the same pattern on the same dates every year, which moving holidays break; the actual holiday dates are knowledge the model can only get from you. Aggregating to yearly totals removes the miss by removing the forecast anyone needed.

drill.q: Before any forecasting model is built, which simple forecasts should you ask for, and why?
drill.a: The same weekday last week, and the average of the last few of that weekday. They are the bar: a model that cannot beat them is not worth having.

drill.q: A forecast has the trend and the weekly rhythm right, but its worst month is twice as bad as its average month. What is probably missing?
drill.a: The known events: holidays, promotions, launches. The rhythm of the data cannot tell a model those dates are special, so you have to supply them.

recall.prompt: Explain to a colleague why 'same as last week' is a respectable forecast, and what a model has to be told to beat it.
recall.model_answer: Copying the same weekday from last week already handles the weekly rhythm, which is most of the day-to-day movement, so it is the baseline any model must beat. To do better, a model has to name what else is in the series: the trend, the time-of-year rhythm, and the dates of known events such as holidays. Those event dates are domain knowledge the data cannot supply by itself. On the simulated series this roughly halved the error, which is a best case because that series is stable and built like the model.

ask_assistant: Forecast [series] for each [day or week] of the next [horizon]. Start with two naive baselines: the same [weekday] one [week] back, and the average of the last [four] of them. Then fit a regression on the log of [series] with a trend, [weekday] effects, time-of-year terms and a flag for each event date in this list: [event dates]. Score every method on the same forecasts: [horizon] ahead from each of the last [twelve] [month starts], each trained only on data before its forecast date. Show, per method, the average error and the worst [month]; list the event dates you used and each forecast's last training date; and report the fitted effects in percent.
audit_checklist: Baselines and model are scored side by side on the same forecast dates
Each forecast shows its last training day, and that day is before the days it predicts
The worst month is reported next to the average
The event dates used are listed, and the fitted trend and weekend effects match your dashboards
transfer: How many support tickets will arrive each day next month, so the team can be staffed?
How many new advertisers will sign up each week next quarter?
How much traffic will a client's landing page get each day over the holiday season?

other_ways.approach: Forecast the big pieces separately and add them up
other_ways.when: When a few verticals or large clients move the total and you know something about their plans.

other_ways.approach: A boosted-tree model on calendar columns
other_ways.when: When rhythms interact in ways a fixed formula cannot express, provided the trend is taken out first or the model predicts growth rather than level: a tree only outputs values it has seen, so on raw levels it under-forecasts a growing series. Judge it against the same baselines: on this series it scored 5.4% over the next 28 days, level with the four-week average.

other_ways.approach: A run-rate from the last four weeks, adjusted by hand for known events
other_ways.when: When the horizon is short, the decision is small and a spreadsheet is all the question deserves.

glossary.def: The slow, persistent rise or fall of a series underneath its ups and downs.
A pattern that repeats on a calendar cycle, such as the weekend dip or the yearly peak in late November.
A forecast that needs no model, such as the same weekday last week; it is the baseline a model must beat.
A dated occasion, such as a holiday or a promotion, whose effect a model can only learn if it is told the dates.
Mean absolute percentage error: the average daily miss as a percentage of that day's actual value.
